reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC & ACC-AHA guidelines
clinicalPearls: Sick sinus syndrome is a spectrum of sinoatrial node dysfunction producing inappropriate bradycardia, sinus pauses or arrest, sinoatrial exit block, and chronotropic incompetence

A common variant is the tachy-brady syndrome, in which paroxysms of atrial tachyarrhythmia (often atrial fibrillation) alternate with symptomatic bradycardia or pauses, especially on termination of the tachyarrhythmia
Symptoms are often intermittent and non-specific, including fatigue, dizziness, presyncope, syncope, and exertional breathlessness from failure of the rate to rise
Because symptoms are paroxysmal, prolonged or ambulatory monitoring is frequently required to correlate them with rhythm disturbances
It is predominantly a disease of older adults from degenerative fibrosis of the sinus node, but drugs, ischaemia, and infiltrative disease can contribute
Reversible contributors such as rate-slowing drugs, hypothyroidism, and electrolyte disturbance should be excluded before attributing symptoms to intrinsic node disease
Permanent pacing is the main treatment for symptomatic bradycardia, and the tachy-brady form often needs both pacing and rhythm or rate control of the tachyarrhythmia
Anticoagulation should be considered when atrial fibrillation coexists, based on thromboembolic risk
reference.pathophysiology: Sick sinus syndrome results from failure of normal impulse generation in the sinoatrial node or failure of conduction from the node to the surrounding atrium. The most common cause is idiopathic degenerative fibrosis of the node and perinodal tissue with ageing. Ischaemia, infiltrative and inflammatory diseases, prior cardiac surgery, and autonomic influences also contribute, and many drugs suppress node function. In the tachy-brady syndrome, atrial remodelling supports tachyarrhythmias, while the diseased node produces prolonged pauses when the tachyarrhythmia stops because of overdrive suppression of an already impaired pacemaker.
additionalDifferentials: Physiological sinus bradycardia (for example in athletes)
AV block and other conduction disturbances
Hypothyroidism and other metabolic causes of bradycardia
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG and prolonged or ambulatory monitoring to correlate symptoms with rhythm
Implantable loop recorder when symptoms are infrequent
Review of rate-slowing medications and thyroid function testing
Electrolyte assessment and evaluation for ischaemia when relevant
Exercise testing to assess chronotropic competence
Echocardiography to evaluate structural heart disease
redFlags: Syncope or recurrent presyncope from prolonged sinus pauses or arrest
Very long pauses, particularly following termination of a tachyarrhythmia in tachy-brady syndrome
Coexisting atrial fibrillation raising thromboembolic and stroke risk
reference.prognosis: Sick sinus syndrome is rarely immediately life-threatening but causes considerable morbidity from recurrent symptoms; pacing effectively relieves bradycardic symptoms, and overall outcome is largely determined by associated atrial fibrillation and thromboembolic risk and by underlying cardiac disease.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to intrinsic node disease without excluding reversible drug or metabolic causes
Failing to capture the arrhythmia because monitoring was too brief for paroxysmal symptoms
Overlooking the need for anticoagulation when atrial fibrillation coexists
Treating bradycardia with pacing while ignoring the tachyarrhythmia component of tachy-brady syndrome
management: Permanent pacemaker implantation, with atrial-based or dual-chamber pacing preferred, as the definitive treatment for symptomatic bradycardia, sinus pauses or chronotropic incompetence
Exclusion and reversal of contributors first, withdrawing rate-slowing drugs, treating hypothyroidism and correcting electrolyte disturbance
Management of the tachy-brady variant with rate or rhythm control of atrial fibrillation, often feasible only once pacing protects against bradycardia
Anticoagulation for thromboembolic risk in associated atrial fibrillation
Ambulatory monitoring or an implantable loop recorder to correlate symptoms with rhythm before committing to device therapy
Treatment of underlying structural or ischaemic heart disease
Escalation to device implantation for recurrent syncope or presyncope attributable to node dysfunction
